data.text/html:
Entropy, explained by playing with it

An interactive companion to DataMListic's video "Entropy - Explained".
Someone picks a number from one to eight. You may ask yes/no questions. How many do you need?
That guessing game leads, in six steps, to one of the central ideas of information theory: surprise → entropy → optimal codes → cross-entropy & KL divergence → maximum entropy. Every section below has something to click, drag or paint.

data.text/markdown:
1 · The guessing game

If all 8 numbers are equally likely, the best strategy is binary search: "Is it in the left half?" → "Is it in the first two?" → "Is it the first one?" Each answer cuts the candidates in half, so you always need exactly ||[\log_2 8 = 3 \text{ questions.}||]But what if some numbers are more likely than others? Then a smart questioner splits the probability mass in half, not the count of candidates, and common numbers get found faster. How to play: the widget secretly draws a number from the bar heights. Click cells to select a set, then press "Is it in my selection?". Eliminated cells turn grey. Or press 🤖 auto to watch the mass-halving strategy play a round. Each finished round is logged to Python.

data.text/markdown:
2 · The measure of surprise

Key insight from the video: rare events carry more information than common ones. A fair coin landing heads? Not very surprising: 1 bit. An event with probability 1/8? 3 bits. ||[I(x) = -\log_2 P(x)||]Why the logarithm? If two events are independent, their surprises should add. Probabilities multiply, ||(P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B)||), and the log turns that multiplication into addition: ||[-\log_2\big(P(A)P(B)\big) = -\log_2 P(A) \;+\; -\log_2 P(B).||]

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet P(A) = 0.5: exactly \u003cstrong\u003e1 bit\u003c/strong\u003e. Set P(B) = 0.125: exactly \u003cstrong\u003e3 bits\u003c/strong\u003e, the video's two examples.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ePush P(A) to 1.0: a certain event has \u003cstrong\u003ezero\u003c/strong\u003e surprise. You learned nothing.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eWatch the red dot: the joint event's surprise is always the sum of the other two. That's the property that \u003cem\u003eforces\u003c/em\u003e the log.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
3 · Expected surprise: the entropy formula

If surprise tells you how informative one outcome is, entropy is the average surprise across all outcomes, each weighted by how often it actually happens: ||[H(X) = -\sum_x P(x)\,\log_2 P(x) = \mathbb{E}\big[-\log_2 P(X)\big].||]Paint a distribution over 8 outcomes below (drag across the bars, or use a preset). The widget shows ||(H||) live; the chart underneath decomposes it into per-outcome contributions ||(P(x)\cdot(-\log_2 P(x))||).

data.text/html: <marimo-ui-element object-id='ZHCJ-0' random-id='908665e5-4260-f2f2-5a46-c7b213b66ab5'><marimo-anywidget data-initial-value='{"model_id":"b95b9691f4a04d8fa56196993a392a1b"}' data-label='null' data-model-id='"b95b9691f4a04d8fa56196993a392a1b"'></marimo-anywidget></marimo-ui-element>

The binary entropy function

For a coin with ||(P(\text{heads}) = p||), the formula simplifies to ||[H_b(p) = -p\log_2 p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p).||]"Look at this curve," says the video: at ||(p=\tfrac12||) (maximum uncertainty) it peaks at exactly 1 bit; at the extremes, when you already know what will happen, it drops to zero.

Uniform is the \u003cem\u003emaximum\u003c/em\u003e for 8 outcomes.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ePress \u003cstrong\u003eVideo: ½ ¼ ⅛ ⅛\u003c/strong\u003e: \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(H = 1.75||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e bits. Remember that number; it returns in Section 4.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ePress \u003cstrong\u003eCertain\u003c/strong\u003e: \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(H = 0||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e. Then paint a tiny bar on another outcome. Note how its grey \u003cem\u003esurprise\u003c/em\u003e tick is huge, but its red \u003cem\u003econtribution\u003c/em\u003e stays small. Rare events are surprising, but they are also rare.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSlide the coin to \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(p = 0.11||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e: the entropy is already only half a bit.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4 · The coding connection

Here's what makes entropy more than a formula: it is the minimum average number of bits needed to encode a message.
  • 4 equally likely symbols → 2 bits each (00 01 10 11), and ||(H = 2||). ✔
  • Probabilities ||(\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18||) → give the common symbol a short code (0) and the rare ones longer codes (10, 110, 111). The average drops to 1.75 bits/symbol, exactly the entropy.
You can't do better: entropy is the theoretical floor (Shannon's source coding theorem). The ideal code length for symbol ||(x||) is its surprise, ||(\ell(x) \approx -\log_2 P(x)||). Below, the codes are built with Huffman's algorithm, which finds the best prefix code for any distribution.

data.text/markdown:
5 · The wrong code: cross-entropy and KL divergence

What if you design your codebook for a distribution Q, but the data actually comes from P? Symbol ||(x||) gets a code of length ||(-\log_2 Q(x)||), but it shows up with frequency ||(P(x)||): ||[\underbrace{H(P,Q) = -\sum_x P(x)\log_2 Q(x)}_{\text{cross-entropy: avg bits under the wrong model}} \qquad \underbrace{D_{KL}(P\,\|\,Q) = H(P,Q) - H(P)}_{\text{wasted bits}} \;\ge 0||]KL is zero only when Q = P. That's why cross-entropy is the loss function everywhere in ML: minimizing cross-entropy pushes your model Q toward the true distribution P. Below, P is the video's ½ ¼ ⅛ ⅛. Set your model Q with the sliders (they get normalized).

data.text/html: Q is rescaled to sum to 1.
Send data from P through both codebooks. The orange code was designed for your Q:

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet all Q sliders equal (uniform model): \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(H(P,Q) = 2||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e, so you waste \u003cstrong\u003e0.25 bits\u003c/strong\u003e per symbol.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet Q to 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125 (proportions 4:2:1:1). KL drops to \u003cstrong\u003e0\u003c/strong\u003e: the right model costs nothing extra.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eBreak it:\u003c/strong\u003e drag Q(A) down to 0.01. The common symbol now gets a ~7-bit code, and KL explodes. Being confidently wrong about frequent events is very expensive.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eCompare the last two stats: \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(D_{KL}(P\\|Q) \\ne D_{KL}(Q\\|P)||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e. KL is a divergence, \u003cstrong\u003enot\u003c/strong\u003e a distance.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
6 · Maximum entropy: the distribution that assumes the least

Given what you know, which distribution should you choose? The one with maximum entropy: it encodes the least extra assumptions beyond your constraints.
  • No constraints (just "one of ||(n||) outcomes") → the max-entropy distribution is uniform.
  • Fixed mean on a die → an exponential tilt ||(P(k) \propto e^{\lambda k}||) (Jaynes' famous dice problem).
  • Fixed mean and variance on the real line → the Gaussian. "The bell curve isn't just convenient; it's the distribution that assumes the least."
First the die: you only know its average roll. Which distribution over 1–6 should you believe?

Fix the mean and variance → the Gaussian

For continuous variables we use differential entropy ||(h(X) = -\int f(x)\log_2 f(x)\,dx||). Every distribution below has mean 0 and variance ||(\sigma^2||). Which one has the most entropy?

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet the die's average to \u003cstrong\u003e3.5\u003c/strong\u003e: the max-entropy answer is exactly \u003cstrong\u003euniform\u003c/strong\u003e (\u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(H = \\log_2 6 ≈ 2.585||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e). No constraint beyond \"fair-looking\", so no extra assumptions.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSlide it to \u003cstrong\u003e4.5\u003c/strong\u003e (Jaynes' example): the answer tilts smoothly toward 6. The two-face guess matches the same mean but invents a strong claim (\"only 4s and 5s happen\"), and its entropy is far lower.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eIn the continuous chart, change σ. The \u003cem\u003eranking\u003c/em\u003e never changes: the \u003cstrong\u003eGaussian is always on top\u003c/strong\u003e. Every curve's entropy shifts by the same \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\log_2\\sigma||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
Recap

Idea Formula One-line intuition Where you played with it
Guessing game ||(\log_2 n||) questions Each yes/no answer halves the uncertainty §1 guessing-game widget
Surprise ||(I(x) = -\log_2 P(x)||) Rare = informative; log makes independent surprises add §2 sliders
Entropy ||(H(X) = -\sum P(x)\log_2 P(x)||) Average surprise; max ||(\log_2 n||) (uniform), min 0 (certain) §3 painter, binary entropy curve
Coding ||(H \le \bar\ell < H + 1||) Entropy is the floor on average bits/symbol §4 Huffman table + encoder simulator
Cross-entropy ||(H(P,Q) = -\sum P\log_2 Q||) Bits you pay using a code built for the wrong model §5 Q sliders, loss curve
KL divergence ||(D_{KL}(P\|Q) = H(P,Q) - H(P) \ge 0||) Wasted bits; 0 iff Q = P; not symmetric §5, sandbox
Max entropy uniform / exp-tilt / Gaussian Choose the distribution that assumes the least §6 die + continuous comparison
"Entropy measures what you don't know, and that turns out to be one of the most useful things you can measure."
